Title: One-Shot Learning using Memory Augmented Neural Networks (MANNs) | by Mehul Gupta | Data Science in Your Pocket | Medium
Data Science in Your Pocket. In my 96th post, we will be discussing how using an NTM as a base, Memory Augmented Neural Networks i.e. MANNs implement One-Shot Learning. > Gives output by reading explicit memory matrix combined with input. > Updates/writes back to memory matrix with updated information. * Instead of reading/writing from specific locations, the controller reads/writes from every location in the memory using weights making the problem differentiable, and hence controller is trainable (a neural network). > **Content based addressing** → How similar is the input with different memory sections using a modified version of cosine similarity. * While generating the Attention Vector (weights for memory rows), we **skip the location-based addressing part.**. * Separate weights are being used for Read and Write operations (the same set of weights are used for both Read & Write in NTMs). * If the current input is similar to rows in the memory matrix, we update recently used memory rows. * But, if the current input is new and has no similarity to any of the memory rows, we update the “Least Recently” used memory locations in the memory matrix hence called LRUA. Let’s first discuss the READ and WRITE operations done by MANNs. > w\_readₜ = read weights at timestamp t. where is w\_readₜ is produced using cosine similarity between input & memory units using the below equation (similar to NTM). Where K() is the cosine similarity function, kₜ is the input and Mₜ is the memory matrix. ### Now the big question is, How are read & write weights getting calculated? The read weights are calculated using the cosine similarity between the memory matrix and current input K as in NTM’s content-based addressing mentioned above. This w\_usageₜ vector basically gives more weightage to memory rows that are recently used (for read and write operations) compared to the one’s not being in use. Here **γ** is constant andw\_readₜ , w\_writeₜ are read & write weights. Now, once this weights\_least\_usedₜ vector is calculated, we would be following a very complex equation to generate w\_writeₜ. As you can observe, basically it’s the w\_write weights that incorporate information about LRUA.

results.title: How does cosine similarity work?
results.content: 2D vectors (that is to say, arrays with only 2 numbers) are much less useful in the context of embeddings, but the same principles apply, and we can use them to illustrate how cosine similarity works. ## Why is cosine similarity useful when comparing vectors? If the directions of the vectors are identical, the cosine similarity is 1. > #### Cosine similarity ignores the magnitude of the vectors. > The cosine similarity formula only cares about the angle between the vectors, not their length. This means that vectors of different lengths can still have a cosine similarity of `1` if they're pointing in the same direction. Now that we've unpicked all the parts of the formula, we can put them together to create a JavaScript function that calculates the cosine similarity of any two vectors. Because cosine similarity measures the similarity of two vectors based on their direction, ignoring their length, it's the perfect tool for comparing embeddings.

Uplatz is a global IT Training & Consulting company. ## Cutting-edge Technology Courses by Uplatz. Home »Infographics»Cosine Similarity Formula – Measuring Text and Vector Similarity. # Cosine Similarity Formula – Measuring Text and Vector Similarity. **🔹 Short Description:** Cosine Similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors, helping determine how similar they are regardless of their magnitude. **Cosine Similarity** is a fundamental metric used to calculate the **similarity between two vectors** in a multi-dimensional space. **Cosine Similarity (A, B) = (A • B) / (||A|| × ||B||)**. * **A • B** is the dot product of vectors A and B. * The result is a value between **-1 and 1**, where:. + **1** means perfectly similar (same direction). + **0** means orthogonal (no similarity). Unlike Euclidean distance, cosine similarity **focuses on orientation, not magnitude**, making it particularly useful in text mining, where two documents may differ in length but still share similar content. * **Chatbots**: Matching user input with known intents. * **Plagiarism detection**: Comparing student submissions for content overlap. * **Recommendation systems**: Suggesting products with similar user profiles. * **Customer segmentation**: Clustering users based on behaviour or preferences. * Cosine similarity helps **normalize for document length**, making it ideal in sparse datasets. * Often used with **TF-IDF vectors** to compare texts. * Supports high-dimensional data comparison with **minimal preprocessing**. * Common in **clustering algorithms** like K-means and in **information retrieval**. * Sensitive to vector construction—**garbage in, garbage out**. * Doesn’t capture **semantic meaning** (e.g., “car” and “automobile” are unrelated). * Requires preprocessing such as stemming, tokenization, and normalization. * In dense vector spaces, results may be less interpretable without dimensionality reduction. * Limited performance in modern NLP compared to **transformer-based embeddings**. Despite these limitations, Cosine Similarity remains a **trusted and efficient tool** for comparing documents, user preferences, or any data represented as vectors in high-dimensional space. **🔹 Meta Title:** Cosine Similarity Formula – Calculate Text Similarity in Vector Space. **🔹 Meta Description:** Explore the Cosine Similarity formula to measure how alike two vectors are, widely used in text mining, recommendations, and NLP. Learn its mathematical basis, practical applications, and advantages in high-dimensional spaces.
